questions.stem: Which sequence correctly traces normal electrical conduction from atria into ventricular myocardium?
options: AV node → SA node → left ventricle → right atrium.
SA node → AV node → His bundle → Purkinje fibres.
SA node → Purkinje fibres → AV node → His bundle.
Purkinje fibres → atria → SA node → AV node.
questions.why: The SA node initiates impulses that reach the AV node, traverse the His–bundle branches and Purkinje system, then depolarise ventricles.

notes.A: The SA node normally initiates atrial excitation.
notes.C: Purkinje fibres come after the AV–His pathway.
notes.D: Ventricular Purkinje fibres conduct after, not before, atrial activation.

questions.stem: A very light stroke briefly leaves a pale line on the skin. How is this reaction best classified?
options: A brief local vasoconstrictor response.
The red line of local capillary dilation.
The spread of an axon-reflex flare.
The wheal component of the triple response.
questions.why: The lecture describes a transient white reaction due to constriction; it is distinct from the classical red–flare–wheal response.

notes.B: The red line is a separate vasodilator response.
notes.C: Flare is surrounding redness from arteriolar dilation.
notes.D: Wheal is raised local oedema from permeability.

questions.stem: A patient with raised intracranial pressure develops hypertension and bradycardia together. What best explains the slow pulse?
options: The hypertension directly activates cardiac beta-1 receptors.
The atrial volume reflex reacts to the sympathetic pressure rise.
The arterial baroreflex reacts to the sympathetic pressure rise.
The cardiac pacemaker stops responding to vagal signals.
questions.why: Medullary ischaemia first raises sympathetic pressure; arterial baroreceptors then increase vagal drive and slow the heart.

notes.A: Β₁ stimulation would usually accelerate, not slow, the heart.
notes.B: Atrial volume receptors respond chiefly to filling, not this sequence.
notes.D: Cardiac autonomic signalling remains central to the response.

questions.stem: A sudden increase in sympathetic venous tone can support cardiac output mainly through which immediate effect?
options: Venoconstriction shifts stored blood centrally.
It dilates veins, increasing blood stored in the limbs.
It creates new circulating plasma within seconds.
It closes arteriolar valves and stops peripheral outflow.
questions.why: Sympathetic venoconstriction reduces the capacity of the venous reservoir and shifts stored blood toward the heart, supporting venous return and end-diastolic filling.

notes.B: Venodilation generally increases peripheral capacitance and pooling.
notes.C: Venoconstriction redistributes existing blood rather than rapidly generating plasma.
notes.D: Systemic arterioles have no valves that close with sympathetic stimulation.

questions.stem: Why can vision fail before consciousness during strong positive acceleration?
options: Retinal perfusion falls as blood shifts toward the feet.
The retina receives blood at higher pressure than the heart.
Intracranial pressure exceeds local arterial pressure.
Positive acceleration shifts blood toward the head.
questions.why: Positive g causes leg pooling and reduced pressure at eye level, so retinal perfusion can fail before cerebral consciousness.

notes.B: Pressure at eye level decreases during positive g.
notes.C: The mechanism is reduced eye-level arterial perfusion, not an inevitable ICP excess.
notes.D: Headward blood movement occurs during negative g.

questions.stem: What most clearly differentiates myocardial infarction from brief stable angina?
options: Stable angina involves transient irreversible injury to the perfused myocardium.
Infarction pain is usually relieved promptly by stopping exertion.
Infarction involves brief ischaemia without permanent myocardial cell damage.
Prolonged ischaemia can produce myocyte necrosis.
questions.why: Prolonged severe ischaemia can cause irreversible myocardial cell death; transient angina does not necessarily cause necrosis.

notes.A: Transient angina ordinarily reflects reversible myocardial ischaemia.
notes.B: Stable angina may result from fixed stenosis without rupture.
notes.C: Infarction can occur across a range of heart rates.

questions.stem: During ventricular diastole, what would an increase in peripheral resistance do to the rate of aortic pressure decline if compliance were unchanged?
options: Reverse arterial flow from capillaries toward the aorta.
Leave the decline unaffected by downstream resistance.
Slow the decline by reducing downstream runoff.
Speed the decline by increasing downstream runoff.
questions.why: Greater downstream resistance reduces diastolic runoff from the elastic arterial reservoir; at unchanged compliance, aortic pressure falls more slowly.

notes.A: Higher resistance slows forward runoff but does not reverse normal arterial flow.
notes.B: Diastolic decay depends in part on resistance and arterial compliance.
notes.D: Greater resistance normally reduces runoff rather than increasing it.

questions.stem: Immediately after rapid loss of a large volume of whole blood, haemoglobin concentration is unexpectedly unchanged. Why?
options: Plasma enters faster than red cells are lost.
Red cells and plasma were lost together.
Erythropoietin instantly makes new red cells.
Red-cell mass increases enough to compensate.
questions.why: Acute whole-blood loss removes red cells and plasma proportionately, so concentration may remain unchanged before fluid replacement.

notes.A: Early dilution has not yet occurred in this scenario.
notes.C: Erythropoiesis takes days to weeks, not minutes.
notes.D: Red-cell mass falls with whole-blood loss.

questions.stem: A drug primarily dilates large systemic veins rather than arterioles. Which immediate circulatory change is most likely?
options: Peripheral resistance rises sharply in the arterioles.
More blood is stored in the venous reservoir.
Capillary smooth-muscle contraction becomes stronger.
More blood is forced towards the right atrium.
questions.why: Venodilation increases capacitance, allowing veins to hold more blood and tending to reduce venous return.

notes.A: Arteriolar tone is the principal determinant of peripheral resistance.
notes.C: Capillaries are not the main contractile vessels.
notes.D: Venoconstriction, not venodilation, mobilises stored blood.

questions.stem: Why can xanthines such as theophylline produce a positive inotropic effect at the signalling level described in the lecture?
options: They directly prevent L-type calcium-channel opening.
They accelerate the breakdown of intracellular cAMP.
They reduce the breakdown of intracellular cAMP.
They block cardiac beta-1 receptor activation upstream of cAMP formation.
questions.why: The lecture describes phosphodiesterase inhibition by xanthines, which slows cAMP breakdown; increased cAMP-dependent signalling can enhance myocardial calcium handling and contractility.

notes.A: Reducing calcium entry would tend to depress rather than enhance contraction.
notes.B: Faster cAMP degradation would reduce this positive inotropic pathway.
notes.D: Blocking beta-1 signalling would generally reduce adrenergic inotropy.

questions.stem: After cord clamping and lung aeration, what pressure change favours functional closure of the foramen ovale?
options: Pulmonary resistance remains very high.
Umbilical venous inflow increases right atrial pressure.
Left atrial pressure exceeds right atrial pressure.
Right atrial pressure rises above left atrial pressure.
questions.why: Increased pulmonary venous return elevates left atrial pressure while loss of placental venous return reduces right-sided filling, pressing the flap closed.

notes.A: Pulmonary resistance falls with first breaths.
notes.B: Clamping removes rather than increases umbilical venous return.
notes.D: Right atrial dominance normally supports fetal shunting, not closure.

questions.stem: During a stress response, circulating adrenaline dilates vessels in working skeletal muscle while constricting many skin vessels. Why?
options: Skin tissue receives a much lower concentration of adrenaline.
Different vascular beds contain markedly different amounts of plasma.
The muscle vessels lack any adrenergic receptors.
Different vascular beds express different adrenergic receptors.
questions.why: β₂ effects can favour dilation in skeletal muscle, while α₁ effects cause constriction in many skin and gut vessels.

notes.A: The difference is due mainly to receptor distribution rather than selective circulating delivery.
notes.B: Plasma volume differences do not explain opposite receptor responses.
notes.C: Muscle vessels respond because they possess adrenergic receptors.

questions.stem: A low-frequency third heart sound occurs in early diastole. What ventricular event coincides with it?
options: Opening of the aortic valve.
Rapid passive ventricular filling.
Isovolumetric ventricular contraction.
Atrial depolarisation before systole.
questions.why: S3 occurs during rapid early-diastolic ventricular filling, as blood entering the chamber causes vibrations.

notes.A: Aortic valve opening occurs during ventricular systole.
notes.C: Isovolumetric contraction occurs near S1.
notes.D: Atrial depolarisation precedes the atrial contribution later in diastole.

questions.stem: Which response becomes particularly important for supporting pressure during sustained rather than momentary upright posture?
options: Renin–angiotensin effects and renal salt retention.
Suppression of aldosterone-driven sodium retention.
Loss of sympathetic arteriolar responsiveness.
Persistent inhibition of all vascular reflexes.
questions.why: The rapid baroreflex stabilizes pressure within seconds, while the renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system supports longer-term pressure and volume.

notes.B: Aldosterone supports sodium retention rather than its suppression.
notes.C: Loss of arteriolar responsiveness would worsen orthostatic control.
notes.D: Baroreflexes remain available during sustained standing.

questions.stem: A patient has hydrocephalus due to impaired absorption by arachnoid villi without an obstructed ventricular pathway. What type is this?
options: Communicating hydrocephalus.
Noncommunicating hydrocephalus.
Isolated ventricular haemorrhage.
Obstructive aqueductal hydrocephalus.
questions.why: Communicating hydrocephalus occurs when CSF reaches subarachnoid space but reabsorption is impaired. The ventricular pathway remains open, so the defect is in absorption rather than transit.

notes.B: Noncommunicating hydrocephalus results from blocked ventricular drainage.
notes.C: Haemorrhage may contribute to hydrocephalus but is not the classification described.
notes.D: Aqueductal stenosis is a specific obstruction.

questions.subtopic: CSF circulation, hydrocephalus and lumbar puncture

questions.stem: What helps maintain forward systemic arterial flow between heartbeats?
options: Capillaries generate contractions that propel blood upstream.
The diaphragm pumps blood through the aorta during inspiration.
Venous valves directly generate aortic pressure.
The elastic recoil of large arteries sustains diastolic flow.
questions.why: Elastic arteries stretch during systole and recoil during diastole, smoothing pulsatile ejection into continuous downstream flow.

notes.A: Capillaries lack the pumping muscle required to drive systemic flow.
notes.B: Respiratory movement mainly assists venous return.
notes.C: Venous valves prevent backflow but do not create aortic pressure.

questions.stem: A recording shows that cardiac vagal stimulation lowers the firing rate of the sinoatrial node. Which additional effect is expected?
options: Stronger ventricular contraction through beta-1 activation.
Faster pacemaker discharge through alpha-1 activation.
Faster impulse conduction through the AV node.
Slower impulse conduction through the AV node.
questions.why: Parasympathetic acetylcholine acts at muscarinic M₂ receptors to slow both SA nodal firing and AV nodal conduction.

notes.A: Β₁ activation describes sympathetic, not vagal, stimulation.
notes.B: The major cardiac pacemaker effect is not mediated by α₁.
notes.C: AV conduction is slowed rather than accelerated by vagal action.

questions.stem: A ventricular depolarisation vector runs almost perpendicular to the viewing axis of a lead. What should that lead record?
options: A prolonged ventricular depolarisation interval.
A small or biphasic ventricular deflection.
A tall upright ventricular deflection.
A tall downward ventricular deflection.
questions.why: Only the component of the electrical vector along the lead axis contributes strongly to the deflection; a near-perpendicular vector has a small projection.

notes.A: Vector orientation changes amplitude and polarity, not necessarily conduction duration.
notes.C: A strongly upright deflection needs a substantial vector component towards the positive pole.
notes.D: A strongly downward deflection needs a substantial vector component away from the positive pole.

questions.subtopic: QRS, ST, T and U waves

questions.stem: A patient with severe tricuspid regurgitation has a prominent systolic jugular venous wave. Which wave becomes especially large?
options: x descent.
v wave.
a wave.
y descent.
questions.why: Tricuspid regurgitation sends systolic flow back into the right atrium and systemic veins, producing a large v or fused c-v wave.

notes.A: The x descent may be blunted rather than unusually enlarged.
notes.C: The a wave reflects atrial contraction and is not the characteristic regurgitant finding.
notes.D: The y descent is an emptying phase and does not represent systolic backflow.

questions.stem: In severe haemorrhagic shock, why does sympathetic constriction of splanchnic vessels help initially?
options: It redistributes flow and mobilises stored venous blood.
It increases hepatic oxygen extraction to 100%.
It increases flow to the intestinal mucosa above baseline.
It prevents all intestinal ischaemia during shock.
questions.why: The splanchnic bed is a large blood reservoir; vasoconstriction redirects perfusion and recruits stored blood toward central circulation.

notes.B: Extraction is not necessarily complete.
notes.C: Mucosal flow may decrease, risking ischaemia.
notes.D: Severe or prolonged constriction can contribute to intestinal injury.

questions.stem: How can impaired coronary perfusion create a vicious cycle during severe shock?
options: Myocardial hypoxia lowers arterial resistance enough to compensate.
Low coronary blood flow increases myocardial ATP stores.
Reduced stroke volume directly increases coronary perfusion pressure.
Coronary ischaemia weakens contraction, further reducing output.
questions.why: Coronary ischaemia depresses myocardial contractility, lowering output and pressure, which further compromises myocardial blood supply.

notes.A: Lower resistance cannot fully resolve a collapsing pump.
notes.B: Ischaemia reduces rather than increases available myocardial ATP.
notes.C: Lower cardiac output tends to worsen coronary perfusion, not restore it.

questions.stem: A patient's right ventricular pumping fails and right atrial pressure rises. Which consequence is most likely?
options: A larger pressure gradient for systemic venous return.
Reduced congestion in peripheral systemic veins.
Reduced venous return gradient with congestion.
Complete disappearance of the jugular venous pulse.
questions.why: Higher right atrial pressure opposes venous return and transmits backward into systemic veins, causing congestion.

notes.A: Higher right atrial pressure reduces the upstream-to-atrial gradient.
notes.B: Elevated atrial pressure tends to increase congestion.
notes.D: JVP often becomes elevated rather than disappearing.

questions.stem: A small additional deflection appears after the T wave in an otherwise interpretable trace. Which description fits the U wave?
options: Atrial depolarisation occurring before the next P wave.
A possible late ventricular repolarisation phenomenon.
Rapid ventricular depolarisation immediately before QRS.
A ventricular plateau interval between QRS and T.
questions.why: The lecture describes a U wave, when seen after T, as the final remnants of ventricular repolarisation. Its precise physiological origin is uncertain.

notes.A: Atrial depolarisation is the P wave preceding QRS.
notes.C: Rapid ventricular depolarisation is represented by QRS, not U.
notes.D: The ventricular plateau is associated with the ST segment.

questions.subtopic: QRS, ST, T and U waves

questions.stem: Why does positioning an accelerating pilot more horizontally improve tolerance to positive g?
options: It increases the distance between the heart and brain.
It shortens the heart-to-brain hydrostatic column.
It raises the capillary filtration rate in the legs.
It directs pooled blood toward the ankles.
questions.why: A more horizontal posture decreases the vertical distance over which acceleration reduces pressure toward the head and brain.

notes.A: Increasing the vertical distance would worsen the gradient.
notes.C: Greater dependent filtration would not protect brain perfusion.
notes.D: Enhanced ankle pooling would reduce central venous return.

questions.stem: A ventricular impulse occurs independently of atrial excitation after complete AV conduction block. What has happened?
options: A subsidiary escape pacemaker has taken over.
Atrial excitation now travels directly through the lungs.
The aortic valves transmit an alternate impulse.
The SA node has increased its firing rate.
questions.why: Complete AV block prevents atrial impulses from reaching ventricles; a slower escape pacemaker may maintain ventricular rhythm.

notes.B: The lungs do not provide an alternative physiological conduction path.
notes.C: Valves do not propagate cardiac electrical impulses.
notes.D: Faster atrial activity alone cannot restore complete AV conduction.

questions.subtopic: AV nodal delay and heart block

questions.stem: Which substance passes relatively readily across the intact blood–brain barrier without a carrier?
options: Plasma albumin.
Carbon dioxide.
A protein-bound drug.
A large immunoglobulin.
questions.why: Small diffusible gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the endothelial membrane relatively easily.

notes.A: Albumin is a large protein with restricted passage.
notes.C: Protein binding reduces free diffusion across the BBB.
notes.D: Large immunoglobulins do not easily cross intact endothelial tight junctions.

questions.stem: During exercise, sympathetic activity increases throughout the body, yet working muscle receives much more blood. Which explanation is best?
options: Local metabolic dilation outweighs constriction in active muscle.
Systemic arteriolar constriction raises every tissue’s flow equally.
A higher systemic pressure redirects flow equally among tissues.
Local metabolic constriction outweighs dilation in active muscle.
questions.why: Active muscle generates enough vasodilator metabolites to oppose sympathetic constriction, redirecting blood to the tissue that needs it.

notes.B: Constriction does not raise flow equally across every organ.
notes.C: Sympathetic activity often remains elevated; metabolites oppose its constrictor effect locally.
notes.D: Metabolites in working muscle predominantly dilate its arterioles.

questions.stem: A patient loses substantial albumin into urine during kidney disease. What Starling-force change is expected?
options: Increased red-cell viscosity causing filtration.
Increased plasma colloid osmotic pressure.
Reduced plasma oncotic pressure promotes oedema.
Reduced capillary permeability everywhere.
questions.why: Proteinuria reduces circulating albumin and its inward oncotic force, favouring movement of fluid into interstitium.

notes.A: Viscosity is not the principal mechanism of protein-loss oedema.
notes.B: Albumin loss lowers oncotic pressure.
notes.D: Capillary permeability elsewhere need not decrease.

questions.stem: A patient becomes dizzy on standing after starting a sympatholytic drug. Which compensatory response is most directly weakened?
options: Constriction of systemic arterioles and veins.
Contraction of calf muscles during walking.
Dilatation of cerebral vessels by carbon dioxide.
Flow of blood through competent venous valves.
questions.why: Sympatholytic drugs blunt reflex arteriolar and venous constriction, so the circulation cannot adequately oppose blood pooling and falling arterial pressure on standing.

notes.B: Walking uses a mechanical muscle pump, not this autonomic drug pathway.
notes.C: Cerebral metabolic vasodilatation is not directly a sympathetic vasoconstrictor response.
notes.D: Venous valve directionality is mechanical and not directly abolished by sympatholytic drugs.

questions.stem: Cardiac beta-adrenergic stimulation raises coronary flow overall mainly through which chain?
options: Direct beta stimulation → closure of coronary arterioles.
More contraction → less ATP use → less adenosine.
More work → metabolites → arteriolar dilation.
Less contraction → less oxygen use → greater vascular tone.
questions.why: Sympathetic stimulation raises cardiac work and oxygen demand; local metabolites then increase coronary perfusion despite competing vasomotor effects.

notes.A: Coronary flow is not increased by closing the arterioles.
notes.B: Greater work increases, not reduces, ATP consumption.
notes.D: Reduced contraction is not the expected beta-mediated cardiac response.

questions.stem: In a whole-body Fick measurement, which blood should the return-side oxygen sample represent?
options: Blood in a single peripheral venule.
Capillary blood from active skeletal muscle only.
Mixed venous blood entering the lungs.
Oxygenated blood in a systemic artery.
questions.why: A mixed venous sample from pulmonary artery reflects oxygen after extraction across the whole body.

notes.A: One local vein does not represent average whole-body extraction.
notes.B: Active muscle has unusually high local extraction and can misrepresent the body.
notes.D: Arterial blood provides the other concentration in the equation.

questions.stem: A patient has had high arterial pressure for months. Why might baroreceptors fail to drive pressure back to the original baseline?
options: Their stretch sensitivity increases indefinitely without adaptation.
Their afferent pathways turn into motor pathways over time.
Their signals stop entering the medulla during hypertension.
Their operating range resets around the sustained level.
questions.why: When pressure stays high for days, the baroreceptors reset and treat the new level as normal, so they defend it instead of correcting it. Long-term pressure is set mainly by the kidneys’ control of salt and water.

notes.A: Unbounded sensitivity would strongly oppose the persistent rise.
notes.B: Sensory fibres do not become motor fibres.
notes.C: Resetting does not require loss of every afferent signal.

questions.stem: Why is a distinct atrial repolarisation wave usually absent from a normal ECG?
options: Atrial repolarisation coincides mainly with the ST segment, where it is too small to detect.
Atrial repolarisation generates no electrical voltage differences.
Atrial repolarisation occurs just before the SA node starts the next beat.
Its small electrical signal is obscured by the ventricular QRS complex.
questions.why: Atrial repolarisation occurs around the time of ventricular depolarisation; the much larger QRS electrical signal masks it on the surface trace.

notes.A: Atrial repolarisation does not need to await the beginning of ventricular diastole.
notes.B: Repolarisation does generate voltage differences, although the signal is small.
notes.C: That statement does not explain why the wave is not separately visible.

questions.subtopic: QRS, ST, T and U waves

questions.stem: Which condition is most likely to depress myocardial contractility rather than enhance it?
options: Raised circulating catecholamines.
Severe hypoxia with acidosis.
Increased calcium availability in cells.
Acute beta-1 adrenergic activation.
questions.why: Severe hypoxia and acidosis impair myocardial function and are listed as causes of depressed inotropy.

notes.A: Catecholamines usually raise inotropy initially.
notes.C: Increased cytosolic calcium generally enhances contraction.
notes.D: Beta-1 activation generally enhances contractility.

questions.stem: A stiff ventricle has high filling pressure but a preserved ejection fraction. What is the primary defect?
options: Increased contractility and ejection.
Impaired relaxation and filling.
Reduced electrical activation of the SA node.
Excessive ventricular compliance.
questions.why: Diastolic failure reflects impaired relaxation and stiff ventricular filling; the fraction of blood ejected can remain normal despite elevated filling pressures and reduced filling volume.

notes.A: Increased contractility is not the primary defect.
notes.C: SA-node dysfunction does not define diastolic heart failure.
notes.D: A stiff ventricle has reduced, not excessive, compliance.

questions.stem: A patient with coronary atheroma is comfortable at rest but develops exertional chest pain. Which explanation fits best?
options: The narrowed artery fully dilates to match any increase in cardiac demand.
A faster heart rate prolongs the diastolic time available for coronary flow.
Sympathetic stimulation lowers myocardial oxygen need during exercise.
Restricted coronary flow reserve cannot meet increased demand.
questions.why: A narrowed vessel may deliver adequate resting flow but cannot dilate enough to meet exercise demand, causing reversible ischaemia.

notes.A: Plaque does not disappear with exertion.
notes.B: Exercise raises myocardial work and oxygen requirements.
notes.C: Resting coronary flow may be sufficient despite reduced reserve.

questions.stem: What does the normal jugular venous 'v' wave mainly represent?
options: Atrial filling while tricuspid is closed.
Closure of the pulmonary semilunar valve.
Right atrial electrical depolarisation.
Completion of left ventricular ejection.
questions.why: Systemic venous return fills the right atrium during ventricular systole while the tricuspid valve remains closed, creating the v wave.

notes.B: Pulmonary valve closure is near S2.
notes.C: Atrial depolarisation precedes the a wave.
notes.D: The v wave is defined by right atrial filling rather than aortic ejection.

questions.stem: Electrical stimulation of the medullary pressor area increases arterial pressure. What is the principal neural pathway?
options: Direct stimulation of the carotid sinus sensory fibres.
Direct inhibition of firing in the sinoatrial pacemaker.
Excitation of sympathetic neurons in the spinal cord.
Inhibition of sympathetic neurons in the spinal cord.
questions.why: The pressor area sends excitatory fibres down to the sympathetic neurons in the spinal cord. More sympathetic output constricts arterioles and veins and speeds and strengthens the heart, so pressure rises.

notes.A: Carotid sinus fibres carry sensory information towards the medulla.
notes.B: Pressor-area activity does not require direct pacemaker inhibition.
notes.D: Inhibiting sympathetic neurons would tend to lower pressure.

questions.stem: A standard ECG uses ten skin electrodes but produces twelve electrical views. How is this possible?
options: The limb electrodes are relocated to the chest during every cardiac cycle.
Several leads are calculated from combinations of the same electrode voltages.
Two extra electrodes inside the heart are automatically activated for recording.
Each electrode produces one lead, with two more produced by blood-pressure sensors.
questions.why: A lead is an electrical viewpoint calculated from one or more electrode potentials, so ten physical contacts can generate twelve different standard recordings.

notes.A: The limb contacts remain in place during a standard recording.
notes.C: Routine twelve-lead ECG does not require intracardiac electrodes.
notes.D: All twelve are electrical leads; pressure sensors do not generate extra leads.

questions.stem: Why do Purkinje fibres help the two ventricles contract as coordinated pumps?
options: They create the calcium plateau in ventricular working myocytes.
They slow ventricular excitation until the semilunar valves can open.
They generate most of the delay between atrial and ventricular activation.
They rapidly activate ventricular myocardium.
questions.why: Rapid His–Purkinje conduction activates much of ventricular myocardium in a short time for synchronised pumping.

notes.A: The key AV delay occurs before the His–Purkinje network.
notes.B: Purkinje fibres primarily serve ventricles, not the atrial septum.
notes.C: Pulmonary valve closure occurs after ventricular ejection.

questions.stem: During standing, head-level arterial pressure falls by 30 mmHg and cerebral venous pressure falls by 25 mmHg. How does arterial minus venous driving pressure change?
options: It falls by about 25 mmHg.
It rises by about 5 mmHg.
It rises by about 55 mmHg.
It falls by about 5 mmHg.
questions.why: The arterial–venous difference changes by −30 minus −25, or −5 mmHg. Falling venous and intracranial pressures therefore help protect cerebral perfusion.

notes.A: That ignores the fall in cerebral venous pressure.
notes.B: The difference becomes slightly smaller, not larger.
notes.C: The changes cannot be added as two rises.

questions.stem: An irregular tracing contains eleven QRS complexes in a six-second span. What is the estimated average ventricular rate?
options: 66 beats/min.
110 beats/min.
90 beats/min.
100 beats/min.
questions.why: Six seconds is one tenth of a minute. Eleven QRS complexes over that span give an approximate average ventricular rate of 11 × 10 = 110 beats/min.

notes.A: This multiplies the QRS count by six, not by ten.
notes.C: A rate of 90 beats/min would correspond to nine complexes in six seconds.
notes.D: A rate of 100 beats/min would correspond to ten complexes in six seconds.

questions.stem: Beta-1 adrenergic stimulation generally increases ventricular contractility through which sequence?
options: Reduced cAMP → less calcium entry → weaker contraction.
Increased vagal tone → reduced pacemaker slope → stronger contraction.
Increased cAMP/PKA signalling → greater calcium availability.
Blocked ryanodine receptors → larger systolic calcium release.
questions.why: Beta-1 signalling raises cAMP and PKA activity, enhancing calcium entry and cycling for stronger contraction.

notes.A: Beta-1 stimulation raises, not lowers, cAMP.
notes.B: Vagal slowing is not the main ventricular inotropic pathway.
notes.D: Blocking release channels would reduce systolic calcium release.

questions.stem: Why can some bronchial venous drainage slightly lower oxygen content of blood reaching the left atrium?
options: Bronchial venous drainage enters only systemic veins, avoiding pulmonary mixing.
Bronchial arteries arise from the pulmonary trunk and deliver deoxygenated blood.
All bronchial venous drainage rejoins systemic arteries before entering the lungs.
Some bronchial venous blood joins pulmonary veins.
questions.why: Some bronchial venous return enters pulmonary veins, mixing a small amount of deoxygenated blood with oxygenated pulmonary venous blood.

notes.A: Not all bronchial venous blood returns only through systemic veins.
notes.B: Bronchial arteries arise from the systemic arterial circulation.
notes.C: Normal pulmonary blood passes through alveolar capillary networks.

questions.stem: What can follow when the right ventricle fails to deliver adequate forward flow to the lungs?
options: Pulmonary flow rises despite low right ventricular output.
Less blood reaches the left heart for systemic output.
Systemic tissues receive more oxygen-rich blood immediately.
Left ventricular filling necessarily increases sharply.
questions.why: Reduced right ventricular output limits pulmonary flow and subsequent return to the left atrium, compromising left-sided filling and delivery.

notes.A: The right heart cannot deliver excess flow when severely failing.
notes.C: Reduced pulmonary transit cannot raise systemic oxygen delivery.
notes.D: Less pulmonary venous return tends to decrease left-sided filling.

questions.stem: What event ends isovolumetric contraction and begins ventricular ejection?
options: Ventricular pressure exceeds the outflow artery pressure.
Atrial contraction briefly increases end-diastolic volume.
Ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure.
Ventricular pressure falls below atrial pressure.
questions.why: Semilunar valves open when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic or pulmonary arterial pressure. The pressure reversal is the immediate mechanical trigger for valve opening.

notes.B: Atrial systole precedes isovolumetric contraction.
notes.C: Lower ventricular than aortic pressure holds the aortic valve closed.
notes.D: This pressure relation opens the AV valves during filling.

questions.stem: A student calls the entire PR interval “the AV nodal delay.” What important part of the interval does this description miss?
options: The delay between ventricular systole and valve opening.
The period during which the ventricular myocardium is repolarising.
The time between the end of QRS and the start of T.
The spread through atria and conduction towards the ventricles.
questions.why: PR includes the P wave itself and conduction through atrial tissue, AV node and His–Purkinje system before QRS begins. AV nodal delay is only one component.

notes.A: Mechanical valve events are not boundaries of the PR interval.
notes.B: Ventricular repolarisation is represented by T and included in QT.
notes.C: End-QRS to start-T corresponds to the ST segment.

questions.stem: A brief sharp pain raises a patient’s pressure, but prolonged severe pain later causes faintness. What best accounts for the difference?
options: Early venous pooling gives way to strong vasoconstriction.
A brief pressor phase gives way to vasodilation.
Long pain increases total peripheral resistance without limit.
Brief pain reduces sympathetic output from central pathways.
questions.why: The lecture distinguishes the pressor response to short, sharp pain from depressor vasodilation and possible syncope with sustained pain.

notes.A: The directions of vascular changes are reversed in this option.
notes.C: Prolonged pain may produce hypotension rather than unbounded resistance.
notes.D: Short sharp pain can stimulate rather than inhibit pressor activity.

questions.stem: Why may the aortic component of the second heart sound become more prominent in systemic hypertension?
options: Brisk aortic valve closure under higher pressure.
Earlier tricuspid closure following atrial contraction.
Late mitral valve closure during ventricular relaxation.
Reduced pulmonary resistance delaying right ventricular ejection.
questions.why: Higher aortic pressure can produce a louder aortic component (A2) of S2 because aortic valve closure is more forceful.

notes.B: Tricuspid closure contributes to S1, not A2.
notes.C: Mitral closure contributes to S1, not the aortic component of S2.
notes.D: Pulmonary resistance and right ventricular ejection primarily influence P2 timing.

questions.stem: A patient with left-sided heart failure feels breathless when lying flat but improves after sitting up. Why?
options: Sitting up increases venous return from the legs.
Sitting up directly increases pulmonary capillary pressure.
Lying flat shifts peripheral blood toward congested lungs.
Lying flat reduces central blood volume.
questions.why: Supine positioning returns peripheral blood to the thorax; a failing left ventricle cannot handle the extra flow, increasing pulmonary venous congestion.

notes.A: Sitting upright tends to reduce thoracic venous return.
notes.B: A higher pulmonary capillary pressure would worsen breathlessness.
notes.D: Central thoracic volume commonly increases rather than decreases supine.

questions.stem: Arterial pressure increases suddenly and baroreceptor firing rises. What changes first in central reflex control?
options: The SA node starts generating impulses without modulation.
Sensory traffic to the medulla decreases despite added stretch.
NTS activation increases pressor and spinal sympathetic firing.
NTS activation increases depressor and vagal signalling.
questions.why: More stretch → faster baroreceptor firing → more input to the NTS. The NTS excites the depressor area (which inhibits the pressor area) and the vagal neurons, so sympathetic output falls and vagal output rises.

notes.A: The heart remains under autonomic regulation during the reflex.
notes.B: Increased wall stretch increases, rather than decreases, afferent traffic.
notes.C: The reflex suppresses rather than increases sympathetic pressor drive.

questions.stem: How can fluid enter a blind-ended lymphatic capillary when interstitial pressure rises?
options: A central lymphatic heart pumps blood into tissues.
A continuous layer of smooth muscle forces plasma outward.
Overlapping endothelial flaps admit interstitial fluid.
Rigid endothelial junctions prevent all protein entry.
questions.why: Initial lymphatic endothelial flaps allow interstitial fluid and proteins to enter when surrounding pressure exceeds lymphatic pressure.

notes.A: There is no single central lymphatic heart.
notes.B: Initial lymphatic capillaries lack a thick continuous smooth-muscle coat.
notes.D: Initial lymphatics are relatively permeable to interstitial proteins.

questions.stem: Where does the ductus arteriosus carry much fetal right ventricular output?
options: From umbilical vein into inferior vena cava.
Directly from right atrium to left atrium.
From left ventricle into hepatic portal vein.
From pulmonary trunk into descending aorta.
questions.why: High prenatal pulmonary resistance diverts much right ventricular output through ductus arteriosus into the aorta.

notes.A: Umbilical venous diversion occurs at the ductus venosus.
notes.B: Right-to-left atrial passage occurs at the foramen ovale.
notes.C: Left ventricular output does not enter the portal vein.

questions.stem: A person becomes angry during an argument, and both pulse and pressure rise. Which route can initiate this response?
options: Cortical signals acting through the hypothalamus on autonomic centres.
Atrial filling signals acting through the kidneys on increased urine output.
Cerebral CSF signals acting through the ventricles on the heart.
Platelet serotonin acting through capillaries on cardiac pacing.
questions.why: Emotions such as anger begin in the cortex. The cortex drives the hypothalamus, which excites the vasomotor centre, raising sympathetic output so heart rate and blood pressure rise.

notes.B: Renal volume control is too slow and not the primary emotional route.
notes.C: The CSF pathways do not directly account for this autonomic response.
notes.D: Platelet serotonin is a local vascular constrictor, not the main emotional signal.

questions.stem: A local inflammatory mediator increases postcapillary venular permeability. What occurs?
options: More protein and water can escape, promoting tissue swelling.
Capillary filtration stops until arterial pressure rises.
The plasma protein concentration increases within the vessel.
The vascular wall becomes impermeable to water.
questions.why: Higher permeability permits protein extravasation and fluid movement, weakening oncotic retention and promoting oedema.

notes.B: Fluid escape is promoted, not stopped.
notes.C: Protein leakage tends to lower intravascular protein in the affected region.
notes.D: Inflammation generally increases rather than abolishes permeability.

questions.stem: What role do arteriovenous anastomoses serve in fingers and other exposed skin?
options: They prevent sympathetic regulation of skin perfusion.
They transfer blood directly into lymphatic capillaries.
They provide adjustable shunts for heat exchange.
They divert blood away from skin when core body temperature rises.
questions.why: AV anastomoses can vary cutaneous blood delivery and heat transfer according to thermoregulatory needs.

notes.A: Skin shunts are under autonomic control.
notes.B: They connect arteries and veins rather than blood to lymph.
notes.D: Their opening and closing vary with temperature regulation.

questions.stem: A measured QRS occupies 3.5 small squares at 25 mm/s. Which statement is supported by the lecture’s usual duration range?
options: It lasts 0.10 s and is at the upper edge of the stated range.
It lasts 0.07 s and is within the stated usual range.
It lasts 0.14 s and is longer than the stated usual range.
It lasts 0.35 s and is longer than the stated usual range.
questions.why: At 25 mm/s, 3.5 small squares equal 3.5 × 0.04 = 0.14 s, above the lecture’s usual QRS duration of 0.06–0.10 s.

notes.A: 0.10 s corresponds to 2.5 small squares at the standard speed.
notes.B: 0.07 s incorrectly halves the 0.14-s measured duration.
notes.D: 0.35 s does not follow from the standard 0.04-s small-square duration.

questions.stem: Where is the largest controllable fall in systemic vascular pressure normally produced?
options: Within the right atrium alone.
Across large elastic arteries.
Across the venae cavae.
Across resistance arterioles.
questions.why: Small arteries and arterioles provide substantial resistance, producing a major pressure drop from arterial to capillary levels.

notes.A: Right atrial pressure is low but does not create the main distributed arterial drop.
notes.B: Large elastic arteries conduct flow with relatively small resistance.
notes.C: Large veins carry blood at low pressure and resistance.

questions.stem: Which combination correctly characterises isovolumetric ventricular contraction?
options: All valves closed, ventricular pressure rises, volume fixed.
All valves closed, ventricular pressure falls, volume fixed.
AV valves open, semilunar valves shut, volume falls.
AV valves open, semilunar valves open, volume rises.
questions.why: Both ventricles generate rising pressure with all inlet and outlet valves closed, so neither receives nor ejects blood.

notes.B: Falling pressure describes isovolumetric relaxation, not contraction.
notes.C: AV valves do not remain open once ventricular pressure rises above atrial.
notes.D: Open valves permit volume exchange.

questions.stem: What closes the aortic valve at the beginning of ventricular relaxation?
options: Venous pressure exceeds aortic pressure.
Atrial pressure rises above left ventricular pressure.
Aortic pressure exceeds ventricular pressure.
Left ventricular pressure rises above aortic pressure.
questions.why: When ventricular pressure falls below aortic pressure, brief reversal tendency closes the aortic valve and starts isovolumetric relaxation.

notes.A: Venous pressure does not directly determine aortic valve closure.
notes.B: Atrial pressure governs mitral opening, not aortic closure.
notes.D: Ventricular pressure exceeding aortic pressure opens the valve.
